elements.text: More good stuff today. Decided to do the work to buffer and total outgoing data per channel. This is the basis of the DoS strategy that was put off forever. Turned out to be super simple. No change to the channel/proxy public interfaces, as it remains just asynchronous. Handlers still invoked in order for each queued write. It's just that they are queued in a deque as opposed to the opaque asio work buffer. This also closes an issue that probably existed with interleave of large (>64k, at least on Win32) writes on a given channel. It's all there now, including the config, tracking of total send and current backlog, log messages, etc. Just need to decide on the formulation for channel dropping based on buffer excess and peer rate limit.

Worked off some technical debt in address pool management today. This included adding services and timestamps to address pool serialization/deserialization, which required a new config::address class (these classes wrap objects to provide command line and settings file parsing, but in this case for the hosts file. Now we can avoid connecting to hosts with insufficient services, which will reduce effective connection time (by not wasting connections), which is a material factor in initial block download.

Also implemented checkout/in of addresses form the pool. This reduces the instances of attempting connection to hosts we are already connected to, which will also reduce effective connection time.

Actually we get pretty good connection time regardless, almost instant, because of batch connection. But this will allow us to reduce the batch quantity to achieve the same rate. Probably from 10 down to 5 or less concurrent attempts per intended outbound connection.

elements.text: Finally found a legit issue in the network stack. The three main session types (inbound, outbound, manual) have a timer (from session base) embedded in the main retry loop, to prevent tight looping in the case of conditions like network offline, no addresses, etc. But the timer is a member of the session, so it has one clock. This gets reset each time there is a new failure event. That's common in the case of these failures, because sessions manage groups of connection attempts. So I need to rethink the approach to these delays, or just remove them. They are mitigated somewhat by the fact that each action is posted to the p2p (network or node) strand.

elements.text: The only approach that I can think of that makes sense is to create a timer for each event, register timer cancel with the stop subscriber, and capture the timer in its stop and timeout handlers. This keeps stop responsive and allows for a delay on each manual connect failure and batch connect failure, and won't get reset by any other events. This also allows the session member timer to be removed. Th overhead shouldn't be an issue, as the whole point is intentional idling.

elements.text: Looking at the per connection sizing, it's about 60kb per connection. Most connections receive a maximally-sized address message, which resizes the incoming buffer to 30kb, so half of the per channel memory is this. elements.text: The reason this matters (a lot) to initial block download performance is that we want to always find the fastest available peers. Diversity doesn't matter in terms of block fill. That's only important for discovery of the header chain (which is not optimized for fast peers). To find faster peers you drop the slow ones and try another. The time spent waiting on another is costly, and if too long ends up requiring that you just maintain more channels, but this causes more work factoring. As I found in prototyping work, getting channels quickly makes a big difference. But I was never able to operate at this density before. With batches of 100 we can establish a connection almost instantly.

Worked on consolidation and better organization of subscribers, possible from the creation of the "resubscriber" template, which allows dropping of subscriptions, and targeting notification to one element by id. Was able to consolidate the session stop, retry and connection-pending subscribers into just one stop subscriber.

This took a good amount of refactor so that sessions and channels are constructed with unique identifiers that can be used for desubscription. But came out better/simpler as a result. connectors/accepter now create only running sockets, not channels. Channels are now created after socket is obtained and verified (blacklist, etc) by session. Session then encapsulates the socket in channel, as before but now in one place (session base) vs. connector and acceptor.

Now that this is done, I can finally remove the last vector of objects (channels) that's being retained by any class for enumeration. I'll create a message broadcaster object, based on the resubscriber. This will allow channels to subscribe for the message types to relay, instead of exposing this publicly for p2p to push through. This will then be symmetrical with incoming message type subscription and will simplify more complex protocol design. Been wanted this change for a long time.

Been working off some technical debt. We have three places where we fan out asynchronous operations and have to resynchronize them. This is a little different than startup/shutdown, because sessions and channels are never really recombined, they just are terminated and the process waits on threadpool join. When the threadpool is continuing it's a different model. I have dealt with this before, but never satisfactorily.

Just finished up three small templates that provide similar but distinct capability for this. I call these racers. I have looked at boost asio tools for this in the past but never found anything that was quite right. These are tools that operate on a single common strand, with asynchronous events (like timer, connect, accept, cancel) moving handlers to a strand for ordered execution. So there's no issue with actual concurrency, just a need to convert multiple events into one handler invoke based on various criteria. Each accepts a hander on start and fires it upon being invoked with completion arguments a certain number of times and/or with certain values.

So I have a "speed racer" that invokes the handler after template N finishes, passing the arguments of the first. IOW the first finisher wins (and should cancel the others) but the invoke doesn't occur until all are finished. Also a "quality racer" that invokes after parameter N finishes, with the first successful finisher winning (getting its arguments passed on). And finally a "volume racer", with a "complete" handler invoked when all N have finished, and a "sufficient" handler invoked as soon as a volume (such as count of connections) is reached.

These are used in the
connector
(speed race between timer and socket connect),
session_outbound
(quality race between a set of connectors, with the first successful connection winning), and
session_seed

(volume race, completing when all seed nodes close and sufficient when a target number of addresses is obtained - or all nodes are closed). These then can be easily fully tested and reduced some longstanding complex code to trivial, just a couple lines in each usage. All working well, tests almost done.

elements.text: The catch with console input is always that the console input needs to terminate the input, since reading from
std::istream
is always a blocking call and there's no way to unblock it. Terminating absent a successful read implies thread termination, which is process corrupting. So the
capture
class launches one thread for the blocking read, and another for posting notification and accepting subscriptions via its own internal strand (just like
logger

). These are set to high priority, so accelerate actions posted via the console, such as stop. Since the threads are almost entirely idle, this has no material impact on the process. The only downside is that in the case of a self-termination (i.e. the node decides it must stop), the process cannot terminate. It just await console input in order to unblock the input thread. So it posts a line to the console (via
logger

) to hit <enter> to close.

Otherwise the interface is very clean, just construct on
std:cin&
and subscribe to lines captured from input. It's nice that, at least on win32, a signal such as
<ctrl-c>

causes both an interrupt and an input event, so there is no need to wait on input. And of course if input terminates (e.g. user types "q" <enter>), then the input can terminate as well. So only on self-termination must it wait. The subscription model allows for input to be written back to the log (explicit and controlled echo). I turn of console echo in construct, as otherwise input text gets interleaved with console output and this is presumably not thread safe.

Terminating absent a successful read implies thread termination, which is process corrupting. So the `capture` class launches one thread for the blocking read, and another for posting notification and accepting subscriptions via its own internal strand (just like `logger`). These are set to high priority, so accelerate actions posted via the console, such as stop. Since the threads are almost entirely idle, this has no material impact on the process. The only downside is that in the case of a self-termination (i.e. the node decides it must stop), the process cannot terminate. It just await console input in order to unblock the input thread. So it posts a line to the console (via `logger`) to hit <enter> to close.

Otherwise the interface is very clean, just construct on `std:cin&` and subscribe to lines captured from input. It's nice that, at least on win32, a signal such as `<ctrl-c>` causes both an interrupt and an input event, so there is no need to wait on input. And of course if input terminates (e.g. user types "q" <enter>), then the input can terminate as well. So only on self-termination must it wait. The subscription model allows for input to be written back to the log (explicit and controlled echo). I turn of console echo in construct, as otherwise input text gets interleaved with console output and this is presumably not thread safe.

elements.text: I played a bit with modifying certain configuration settings from the console, which works fine as long as the application adapts to the change. Settings are passed pervasively using a single
const&
though the application. This can be modified by the
node

class owner, though in some cases the use of the setting would require a notification. So eventually the settings class will carry a subscriber, and any class that accepts settings and wants to update on a change can subscribe to change notification. This would then just require that the setting change be notified by type - which we can now do at the console. Eventually this can be done via an zeromq admin interface. I recently removed the channel registration vector, which was required for both stop notification and message broadcast, and replaced it with a de-subscribable (new) stop subscriber. This was a half-step toward creating a broadcaster, to which channels subscribe for both stop notification and messages broadcast from outside the node or across channels. This cleaned up the control inversion of the node maintaining a channel vector, but it left for future work the task of creating the broadcaster.

Today I laid a bunch of the groundwork for the broadcaster. This an analog to the message subscriber (pump), which protocols use to obtain messages incoming from their channel's peer. So I normalized a few things in the pump implementation with the anticipated broadcaster. This also included doing some longstanding work in hash optimization.

Bitcoin p2p performs a double hash on each message and graphs 4 bytes as a checksum, placed into the header. This can be bypassed when reading messages, but is necessary for outgoing - in case another node is validating. For empty messages this is a fixed value, so free. For some messages, the hash is required after reading, and generally available when writing (to the net). This applies most obviously to blocks/headers and txs.

Obtaining the hash from a read is most optimally done via the read buffer. Previously we would reserialize the tx just to get its hash, which is a huge expense. Also, when we get a block/header/tx from the store - we have the hash. So I worked it out a while back that message objects would have the ability to ferry their identity hash and/or checksum, so that we could eliminate all of the redundant and hugely expensive hashing. I just stubbed in the simple remaining changes to eliminate all redundant hashing, and to ferry the hash and/or checksum as applicable for certain message, on a message-by-message type basis.

The consequence is that we will never compute hashes on hash/block/tx objects retrieved from the database for sending on the wire, never serialize an object off the wire to obtain its hash, either for identity or checksum validation, never compute a hash redundantly (for both checksum validation and identity), and never compute a hash/checksum for a message that is read and then forwarded.

I contemplated storing checksums in the database for certain message types, but the storage cost is large and there is no advantage for header/block/tx objects, as the checksum is a cast of the database natural key. There really aren't any other p2p message types for which it could be stored.

elements.text: So once I've completed this optimization, I'll finish up the message broadcaster. This object presents an interesting question. A broadcast message should be serialized once for all peers, as there may be many and reserialization for each is costly. Previously we serialized for each peer. So imagine, with 10 peers, each rebroadcast tx was serialized to a buffer for each peer
and

each was serialized again to obtain its hash - for each peer - to obtain the network checksum. Where N is peer count, that's 2*N (vs. 1) serializations and N double hashes (vs. 0) for each broadcast tx.

But our message serialization is purposely protocol version dependent, as there are cases where protocol may vary serialization. This means that each channel can potentially require independent serialization. Fortunately the need for this is limited, and we can rely on canonical serialization in most situations. So the broadcaster serializes and then pushes out the buffer (including header/checksum) to each peer for send. But a subscribing protocol may need to inspect the message, and not just forward it blindly. So the original un-serialized object is provided, as well as a buffer - both passed by shared pointer.

This is basically the same as the message pump except that the subscribers are not receiving notifications on their own strand, they are receiving notifications on the singleton network strand - and each must therefore bounce over to its own strand for thread safety. But this doesn't affect the design of the broadcaster (vs. the pump). The main distinction is that, as a subscriber on an independent strand, the protocols/channel must handle completion for subscription in order to not miss messages. But since, unlike channel protocol, broadcast is best effort - this shouldn't be necessary.
